Eggs of the Yellowmouth grouper (Mycteroperca interstitialis), which are pelagic and transparent, hatch after a brief incubation period of approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 19.6 °C [T = 19.6 °C]. The resulting yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with an initial wet weight at birth of roughly 0.00045 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00045 grams], derived from an egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters. This minuscule birth mass, typical of grouper species with pelagic eggs, means the prolarvae embark on an endotrophic phase relying entirely on their yolk reserves. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening, a critical period where first prey capture must succeed to avoid starvation. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of this species is 4% [GSI = 4%] under a thermal regime of 19.6 °C [T = 19.6 °C].

Juvenile Yellowmouth grouper undergo a prolonged period of benthic growth before reaching the size threshold associated with sexual maturation. The total length at which 50% of individuals attain puberty is 42 centimeters [Lp = 42 centimeters], a metric derived from extensive field sampling of sub-adult fish. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 599 grams [Wwp = 599 grams] based on a length-weight relationship calculated for this species. This weight represents a significant increase of several orders of magnitude from the larval stage and reflects the substantial somatic investment required before gonadal recrudescence can begin. The growth trajectory toward reproductive maturity is relatively slow, with individuals typically spending several years accumulating the necessary biomass. Comparative data from related serranids indicate that the length at first maturity in Mycteroperca interstitialis is somewhat intermediate within the genus, consistent with its moderate maximum size.

The ultimate total length achieved by this species has been documented at 84 centimeters [Li = 84 centimeters], representing the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. This measurement was derived from mark-recapture studies and verified against commercial fishery landings. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an adult fish of this length is approximately 4995 grams [Wwi = approximately 4995 grams], a relationship that follows a power-law curve typical of grouper body morphology. This maximum mass places the Yellowmouth grouper among the medium-bodied members of its genus, being considerably smaller than the massive Goliath grouper but notably larger than several of the smaller Epinephelus species that share its reef habitat. The attainment of this ultimate size is a function of both age and environmental conditions, with individuals in productive habitats reaching larger sizes more rapidly than those in marginal environments.

Longevity data for Mycteroperca interstitialis, compiled from otolith-based age readings and tag-return records, indicate a maximum documented lifespan of 41 years [am = 41 years] when reared under the stable temperature conditions typical of its subtropical range (19.6 °C [T = 19.6 °C]). This exceptional longevity is characteristic of many epinephelids and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparous reproduction over a single, high-investment spawning event. The extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, which buffers the population against periodic recruitment failures. In terms of energetic scaling, this longevity aligns with the species’ moderately large body size and slow growth rate during the adult phase. Older individuals, particularly those exceeding 30 years of age, contribute disproportionately to the spawning stock biomass due to their higher fecundity and spawning frequency compared to younger, first-time spawners.

From a comparative physiological and ecological perspective, the life-history of the Yellowmouth grouper exemplifies a k-selected strategy common among large reef predators. The substantial investment per offspring, evidenced by a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00045 grams] despite the planktonic larval phase, and the long lifespan of up to 41 years [am = up to 41 years] under thermal conditions near 19.6 °C [T = 19.6 °C], together with the large adult body size of about 84 centimeters [Li = about 84 centimeters] total length, all point to a species that relies on high adult survival and repeated spawning events to maintain population stability. The gonadosomatic index was 4% [GSI = 4%] at a temperature of 19.6 °C [T = 19.6 °C]. Such traits render the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals—those with the highest reproductive value—can have outsized impacts on population recovery.
